p.src: When Taizong reached him, the man knelt beside the road and said, “Your Majesty, forgive your subject for failing to come farther to welcome you.” Taizong asked, “Who are you? Why have you come to receive me with such obeisance?” The man replied, “Half a month ago, in the Hall of Senluo, your humble subject saw the ghost-dragon of the Jing River accuse Your Majesty of promising to save him but instead having him executed. King Qinguang of the First Court therefore sent ghostly officers to summon Your Majesty so that the case might be heard before the Three Administrations. I learned of this and came here to await and receive you. I did not expect to arrive late today. I beg you to forgive me, forgive me.” Taizong said, “What is your surname and given name? What office do you hold?” The man replied, “While alive, your humble subject served the late emperor in the realm of the living, first as magistrate of Cizhou and later as Vice Minister of Rites. My surname is Cui and my given name is Jue. Now in the netherworld, I serve as the judge in charge of the records of Fengdu.” Taizong was overjoyed. Moreover, he has always watched over my descendants. Above its gate hung a great plaque bearing seven large golden characters: “Ghost Gate Pass of the Netherworld.” The blue-robed boys waved their banners and led Taizong straight into the city and along its streets. Beside the street he saw the late sovereign Li Yuan, his elder brother Jiancheng, and his deceased younger brother Yuanji. They came forward crying, “Shimin has come! p.src: As Taizong watched from outside, he heard jade pendants chiming from the side and caught a wondrous celestial fragrance. Two pairs of attendants bearing candles came first; behind them, the Ten Kings of Hell descended the steps. They were King Qinguang, King Chujiang, King Songdi, King Wuguan, King Yama, King Pingdeng, King Taishan, King Dushi, King Biancheng, and the Wheel-Turning King. The Ten Kings emerged from the precious Hall of Senluo, bent low with bowed backs, and welcomed Taizong. Taizong humbly deferred and dared not go ahead. The Ten Kings said, “Your Majesty is a sovereign among men in the world of light, while we are ghostly kings in the realm of darkness. Our respective stations make this only proper; why be so excessively courteous?” Taizong replied, “I have offended one of your subjects. How could I presume to speak of distinctions between light and darkness, men and ghosts?” Still he continued to defer. At last Taizong went forward and entered the Hall of Senluo. After exchanging courtesies with the Ten Kings, host and guest took their appointed seats.

p.src: After a short while, King Qinguang cupped his hands and said, “The ghost-dragon of the Jing River accuses Your Majesty of promising to save him but instead having him killed. How do you answer this?” Taizong replied, “The old dragon once came to me in a dream to beg for help, and I did indeed promise that no harm would befall him. But unexpectedly, he had committed a capital crime and was sentenced to be beheaded by Wei Zheng, my officer in the human administration. I summoned Wei Zheng to the palace and kept him playing chess, never knowing that he would behead the dragon in a dream. This was the unfathomable divine agency of that officer of the human administration, and the Dragon King had committed a crime for which he deserved death. How can it be my fault?” Hearing this, the Ten Kings bowed low and said, “Before that dragon was even born, the register of death kept by the Southern Dipper had already decreed that he would be slain by an officer of the human administration. We knew this long ago. Yet he persisted in arguing his case here and insisted that Your Majesty be brought here so that the Three Administrations might hear the matter together. We have already sent him into the wheel repository to be reborn. Now we have troubled Your Majesty to descend here as well. We beg you to forgive us for pressing you to come.” When they had finished speaking, they ordered the judge in charge of the registers of life and death to fetch the records at once and determine how many years of earthly life and Heaven-granted reign remained to His Majesty. Judge Cui hurried back to the records office and examined one by one the master register of Heaven-ordained reigns for the rulers of all nations under Heaven. There he found that the entry for Emperor Taizong of the Great Tang in the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa allotted him thirteen years of the Zhenguan era. Judge Cui was startled. He quickly took a thick brush dipped in heavy ink and added two strokes above the character “one,” then presented the register. The Ten Kings read it from the beginning and saw that thirty-three years were allotted beneath Taizong’s name. The Kings of Hell asked in surprise, “How many years has Your Majesty occupied the throne?” Taizong replied, “It has now been thirteen years since I ascended the throne.” The Kings of Hell said, “Your Majesty, set your mind at ease and do not worry. You still have twenty years of earthly life remaining. This inquiry has now made the case clear. Please return to your body and go back to the world of light.” Hearing this, Taizong bowed and expressed his thanks. The Ten Kings of Hell ordered Judge Cui and Grand Commandant Zhu to escort Taizong’s soul back to his body. As Taizong left the Hall of Senluo, he raised his clasped hands and asked the Ten Kings, “Are the old and young in my palace all well?” The Ten Kings replied, “All are well, though we fear your imperial sister may not have long to live.” Taizong bowed again and said in gratitude, “When I return to the world of light, I shall have nothing with which to repay you save an offering of melons and fruits.” The Ten Kings said delightedly, “We have plenty of winter melons and watermelons here; only pumpkins are lacking.” Taizong said, “As soon as I return, I shall send some—indeed I shall.” Thereupon they exchanged bows and parted.

p.src: While they were speaking, the Messengers of the Bridges had already departed. Taizong’s heart again quailed with fear; he nodded and sighed inwardly, grieving in silence. Following the judge and the grand commandant, he soon crossed the foul waters of the River of Woe and the bitter realm of the Basin of Blood. Farther on they came to the City of the Wrongfully Slain. A clamorous crowd could be heard shouting distinctly, “Li Shimin has come! Li Shimin has come!” Hearing the cries, Taizong trembled with terror. He saw a swarm of specters—some bent double, some with broken arms, and some with feet but no heads—rush forward and block his way. They all cried, “Give us back our lives! Give us back our lives!” Taizong panicked and dodged this way and that, crying only, “Master Cui, save me! Master Cui, save me!” The judge said, “Your Majesty, these are the ghosts of the princes and chieftains from the sixty-four theaters of war and the seventy-two bands of rebels. All were wrongfully slain and bear bitter grievances. No one receives or governs them, so they cannot pass on to another birth; and having no spirit money for their journey, they are all destitute, starving ghosts. If Your Majesty gives them some money, only then can I rescue you.” Taizong said, “I came here with nothing on me. Where could I possibly obtain any money?” The judge replied, “Your Majesty, there is a man in the world of the living who has deposited a certain amount of gold and silver here in the underworld. Your Majesty may sign an agreement in your own name, and I shall stand guarantor. Borrow one treasury from him for the moment and distribute it among these hungry ghosts; only then will you be able to pass.” Taizong asked, “Who is this man?” The judge said, “He is from Kaifeng Prefecture in Henan. His surname is Xiang and his given name is Liang. He has thirteen treasuries of gold and silver here. If Your Majesty borrows from him, you need only repay him upon returning to the world of the living.” Taizong was delighted and willingly agreed to borrow it in his own name. He accordingly drew up a document with the judge, borrowed one treasury of gold and silver, and ordered the grand commandant to distribute it all. The judge then instructed them, “Divide this gold and silver equally among yourselves for your needs, and let your lord and master of Great Tang pass. Many years of his allotted life remain. I have received the commands of the Ten Kings and am escorting him back to life. In the mortal world he will hold a Grand Rite of Water and Land to deliver you into new births, so cause no further trouble.” When the ghosts heard this and received the gold and silver, they all murmured assent and withdrew. The judge ordered the grand commandant to wave the soul-guiding banner. Leading Taizong out of the City of the Wrongfully Slain, they set out upon the broad road to the world of light and drifted away.

p.src: The judge escorted the Tang emperor as far as the gate to noble rebirth. Bowing, he called to him, “Your Majesty, this is the place from which you will emerge. I must now take my leave; Grand Commandant Zhu will escort you a little farther.” The Tang emperor thanked him, saying, “You have taken the trouble to come a very long way, sir.” The judge said, “Your Majesty, when you reach the world of the living, you must by all means hold a Grand Rite of Water and Land to deliver those masterless, aggrieved souls. Proclaim universally that the people of the world should do good, and I assure you that your descendants will continue without end and your realm endure forever.”

p.src: The Tang emperor agreed to every proposal, took leave of Judge Cui, and entered the gate together with Grand Commandant Zhu. Inside the gate the grand commandant saw a bay horse with saddle and trappings complete. He hurriedly invited the Tang emperor to mount and supported him at his side. The horse sped like an arrow and soon reached the bank of the River Wei. There upon the water they saw a pair of golden carp leaping and frolicking amid the river’s waves. The Tang emperor was delighted by the sight. He reined in his horse and gazed so eagerly that he could not tear himself away. The grand commandant said, “Your Majesty, make haste! Enter the city early, while there is still time.” But the Tang emperor remained absorbed in watching and refused to go on. The grand commandant seized him by the foot and shouted, “Why are you not going? What are you waiting for?” With a splash, he pushed him from the horse into the River Wei. At once he escaped the underworld and returned directly to the realm of the living.

u.src: The Tang emperor agreed to every proposal, took leave of Judge Cui, and entered the gate together with Grand Commandant Zhu.
Inside the gate the grand commandant saw a bay horse with saddle and trappings complete. He hurriedly invited the Tang emperor to mount and supported him at his side.
The horse sped like an arrow and soon reached the bank of the River Wei.
There upon the water they saw a pair of golden carp leaping and frolicking amid the river’s waves.
The Tang emperor was delighted by the sight. He reined in his horse and gazed so eagerly that he could not tear himself away.
The grand commandant said, “Your Majesty, make haste! Enter the city early, while there is still time.”
But the Tang emperor remained absorbed in watching and refused to go on.
The grand commandant seized him by the foot and shouted, “Why are you not going? What are you waiting for?”
With a splash, he pushed him from the horse into the River Wei.
At once he escaped the underworld and returned directly to the realm of the living.

p.src: Now at the Tang court, the civil and military officials of both ranks—including Xu Maogong, Qin Shubao, Hu Jingde, Duan Zhixuan, Ma Sanbao, Cheng Yaojin, Gao Shilian, Li Shiji, Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Xiao Yu, Fu Yi, Zhang Daoyuan, Zhang Shiheng, and Wang Gui—were all attending the crown prince of the Eastern Palace, the empress, the imperial consorts, palace maids, and senior attendants as they mourned in the White Tiger Hall. Meanwhile, they discussed issuing an imperial proclamation of mourning to inform the whole realm and enthroning the crown prince. At this, Wei Zheng, who stood nearby, said, “Gentlemen, wait. You must not do this—indeed, you must not. If the prefectures and counties are alarmed, I fear some unforeseen disturbance may arise. Wait and observe for one more day. Our sovereign will surely return to life.” Xu Jingzong stepped forward from below and said, “Prime Minister Wei’s words are utterly absurd. Since ancient times it has been said, ‘Spilt water cannot be gathered up, and the dead do not return.’ Why, then, do you utter such empty words to confuse the people’s hearts? What sense is there in that?” Wei Zheng replied, “I will not conceal it from you, Master Xu. Since childhood I have been instructed in the arts of the immortals, and my calculations are exceedingly accurate. I guarantee that His Majesty is not dead.”

p.src: By then, every palace attendant had fled, and none dared approach the bier to support the coffin. Fortunately, the upright Xu Maogong, the resolute Chancellor Wei, the courageous Qin Qiong, and the fiercely impetuous Jingde stepped forward to steady the coffin and called, “Your Majesty, if anything still weighs upon your heart, tell us. Do not play the ghost and frighten your family.” Wei Zheng said, “This is no ghostly trick. His Majesty is returning to life. Quickly, bring some tools!” They opened the coffin lid and indeed saw Taizong sitting within, still crying, “I am drowning! Who will pull me out?” Maogong and the others stepped forward to help him up, saying, “Your Majesty has awakened. Do not be afraid; your servants are all here to protect you.” Only then did the Tang emperor open his eyes and say, “What bitter torment I have just endured! No sooner had I escaped the evil ghosts of the underworld than I met with a watery death.” The ministers said, “Set your mind at ease, Your Majesty, and do not fear. What watery disaster befell you?” The Tang emperor said, “I was riding on horseback and had just reached the bank of the Wei River when I saw two-headed fish playing. Marshal Zhu treacherously pushed me from my horse. I fell into the river and nearly drowned.” Wei Zheng said, “Your Majesty has not yet cast off the aura of the spirit world.” He urgently ordered the Imperial Medical Academy to present a decoction to calm the mind and settle the soul, and had gruel and other food prepared. After taking these once or twice, the emperor finally returned to his former self and regained awareness of the world around him. By the reckoning, the Tang emperor had been dead for three days and nights before returning to the world of light to reign once more. A poem bears witness:

p.src: The Tang emperor ascended the Golden Throne Hall, where the civil and military officials of both ranks assembled. When they had finished their cries of homage, they took their places according to rank. Then the herald proclaimed, “Those with matters to report, step forth; if there is no business, the court shall adjourn.” From the eastern side stepped Xu Maogong, Wei Zheng, Wang Gui, Du Ruhui, Fang Xuanling, Yuan Tiangang, Li Chunfeng, Xu Jingzong, and others; from the western side stepped Yin Kaishan, Liu Hongji, Ma Sanbao, Duan Zhixuan, Cheng Yaojin, Qin Shubao, Hu Jingde, Xue Rengui, and others. Together they came forward, prostrated themselves before the white jade steps, and memorialized, “Your Majesty, in that dream of the previous court day, why did it take you so long to awaken?” Taizong said, “The other day, upon receiving Wei Zheng’s letter, I felt my spirit leave the hall, and then saw the Imperial Guard inviting me to go hunting. As we proceeded, both men and horses vanished, and then I saw my late father the sovereign and my late brothers wrangling with me. Just when matters were most difficult to resolve, a man appeared in a black cap and dark robe. It was Judge Cui Jue, who shouted my late brothers away. I handed Wei Zheng’s letter to him. While he was reading it, I saw attendants in blue holding banners and pennants. They led me inside to the Hall of the Underworld, where I was seated in company with the Ten Kings of Hell. They said that the Dragon of the Jing River had accused me of promising to save him and then having him killed. I set forth the whole truth of the matter to them. They said the case had already been checked against the records of the Three Offices, and urgently ordered the register of life and death brought forth to examine my allotted years in the living world. Judge Cui then presented the register. After examining it, the King of Hell said that I had been granted thirty-three years of Heaven’s favor, of which only thirteen had passed, leaving me twenty more years of mortal life. He therefore ordered Marshal Zhu and Judge Cui to escort me back. I took leave of the Ten Kings and promised to send them melons and fruit in gratitude for their kindness. After leaving the Hall of the Underworld, I saw in the netherworld those who had been disloyal or unfilial, violated propriety and righteousness, wantonly wasted the five grains, cheated openly or in secret, used large measures when buying and small ones when selling, or committed adultery, theft, fraud, deceit, lust, and treachery. Thousands upon thousands suffered the torments of grinding, burning, pounding, and hacking, and the punishments of boiling, scorching, hanging, and flaying—more than I could finish beholding. Passing through the City of Untimely Death, I encountered countless wronged spirits. They were all the souls of bandits from the sixty-four regions of turmoil and rebels from the seventy-two strongholds, and they barred my way. Fortunately, Judge Cui stood surety for me and borrowed a treasury of gold and silver belonging to old Chancellor Xiang of Henan. Only after buying off the ghosts could I proceed. Judge Cui repeatedly charged me that, upon returning to the living world, I must by all means hold a grand Water-and-Land Assembly to deliver those masterless, solitary souls. After we parted and passed beyond the Six Paths of Reincarnation, Marshal Zhu invited me to mount a horse. We traveled as though flying until we reached the bank of the Wei River, where I saw two-headed fish playing on the surface. Just as I was rejoicing, he seized me by the feet and pushed me into the water—and thus I returned to life.” When the ministers heard this account, every one of them offered congratulations. The account was then circulated and proclaimed throughout the realm, and officials of every prefecture and county submitted memorials of celebration. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Taizong then issued another decree granting amnesty to the prisoners throughout the realm. He also ordered an inquiry into the serious offenders in prison. The examining officials reviewed the prisoners condemned by the Ministry of Justice to strangulation or beheading and presented a list of more than four hundred names. Taizong pardoned them long enough to return home, take leave of their parents and siblings, entrust their property to their relatives, sons, and nephews, and report to the authorities on that same day the following year to receive the punishment due to them. The prisoners thanked him for his grace and withdrew. He also issued a proclamation for the relief of orphans. He then counted the old and young palace women, three thousand in all, and decreed that they be released to marry soldiers. From that time onward, goodness prevailed both within the palace and beyond it. A poem bears witness. The poem says:

p.src: After the proclamation had been posted for several days, a worthy man volunteered to carry the melons and fruit. He was a native of Junzhou, surnamed Liu and named Quan, and possessed a fortune worth ten thousand strings of cash. His wife, Li Cuilian, had once removed a golden hairpin at the front gate to give alms to a monk. Liu Quan scolded her, saying that she had failed to observe a wife’s proper conduct by leaving the women’s quarters without permission. Unable to endure her resentment and humiliation, Lady Li hanged herself. She left behind a young son and daughter, who wept day and night. Liu Quan could not bear the sight of them either. Having no other recourse, he resolved to surrender his life, abandon his home and fortune, and leave his children behind. Willing to die in order to deliver the melons, he took down the imperial proclamation and came before the Tang emperor. The emperor issued an order instructing him to go to the Golden Pavilion Hostel, place a pair of pumpkins upon his head, carry spirit money in his sleeves, and hold medicine in his mouth.

p.src: Liu Quan duly took poison and died. His solitary spirit, bearing the melons and fruit, soon arrived at the Gate of Ghosts. The ghostly warder at the gate shouted, “Who are you, to dare come here?” Liu Quan replied, “I come by imperial commission of His Majesty Emperor Taizong of the Great Tang, expressly to present melons and fruit for the Ten Kings of Hell to enjoy.” The ghostly warder gladly received him and led him in. Liu Quan went straight to the Precious Hall of Senluo and, upon seeing the King of Hell, presented the melons and fruit, saying, “By command of the Tang emperor, I have brought these melons and fruit from afar to thank the Ten Kings for the grace of your merciful pardon.” The King of Hell was delighted and said, “What a trustworthy and virtuous emperor Taizong is!” Thereupon, they accepted the melons and fruit. They then asked the name and native place of the man who had brought the offering. Liu Quan replied, “This humble man is registered as a resident of Junzhou City. My surname is Liu and my given name is Quan. Because my wife, Madam Li, hanged herself, leaving our children with no one to care for them, I willingly abandoned home and children and sacrificed my life in service to the realm, expressly to present these melons and fruit on behalf of my king and thank Your Majesties for your great kindness.” On hearing this, the Ten Kings at once ordered that the case of Liu Quan’s wife, Madam Li, be investigated. The ghostly warders quickly brought her before the Hall of Senluo, where husband and wife were reunited. After recounting all that had happened, they thanked the Ten Kings for the grace of their pardon. When the King of Hell consulted the Register of Life and Death, he found that husband and wife alike were allotted the lifespan of those destined for immortality, and hurriedly ordered ghostly warders to send them back. The ghostly warder reported, “Li Cuilian has been in the realm of the dead for a long time, and her corpse no longer exists. To what body can her soul return?” The King of Hell said, “The Tang emperor’s younger sister Li Yuying is now due an untimely death. You may borrow her body and let this woman’s soul return to life in it.” The ghostly warder accepted the command and at once took Liu Quan and his wife to be restored to life; together they departed from the realm of the dead.
